theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. You may use a calculator unless the instructor says otherwise. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: You are about to work out a cut list from a drawing. What should you do first?
options: Round every size on the drawing to the nearest 10 mm
Check the sizes and change them all to the same unit
Order the steel so it arrives before you start
Add 10% to every size on the drawing to be safe

questions.stem: An old drawing asks for 3/8 inch plate. What is this in millimetres, to one decimal place? (1 inch = 25.4 mm)
Work out 2 1/2 − 3/4.
A bolt diameter is given as 0.625 inch. Which fraction of an inch is this?
A selling price of J$11 500 includes a 15% mark-up on the cost. What was the cost?
A job is estimated at 32 hours. The supervisor adds 15% for setting up and cleaning up. How many hours are planned?
Kemar is paid J$900 an hour. Overtime is paid at time and a half. What does he earn for 6 hours of overtime?
Four welders take 6 days to finish a set of gates. Working at the same rate, how long would three welders take?
A team makes 45 brackets in 3 hours. At the same rate, how many complete brackets will it make in a 7.5-hour shift?
A profit of J$84 000 is shared between two partners in the ratio 3 : 4. What is the larger share?
A job needs 27.3 m of angle in total. The angle comes in 6 m lengths. Ignoring waste and how the pieces fit, how many lengths must be ordered?
Pieces 460 mm long are cut from a 6 m bar. Each saw cut wastes 4 mm, and every piece needs one cut. How many complete pieces can be cut?
Twelve pieces of 460 mm are cut from a 6 m bar, with 4 mm lost at each of the 12 cuts. How long is the offcut left over?
How many blanks 300 mm × 200 mm can be cut from a 1200 mm × 2400 mm sheet, ignoring the width of the cuts?
Blanks 350 mm × 250 mm are cut from a 1200 mm × 2400 mm sheet, all set the same way round. What is the most blanks you can get, ignoring cut widths?
An L-shaped base plate is a 600 mm × 400 mm rectangle with a 200 mm × 200 mm square cut from one corner. What is its area?
A slot is 80 mm long overall and 20 mm wide, with fully rounded ends. What is the length of the cut round it? (π = 3.142)
A ring is rolled from 10 mm thick flat bar to an inside diameter of 500 mm. Using the mean diameter, what length of bar is needed? (π = 3.142)
Eight bolt holes are spaced equally round a pitch circle. What angle is there between the centres of two holes next to each other?
What is the size of each inside angle of a regular hexagon (six equal sides)?
Two angles of a triangular gusset are 90° and 35°. What is the third angle?
Five holes are to be spaced equally along a 1200 mm bar, with the two end holes each 100 mm in from the ends. What is the spacing between hole centres?
A round water tank is 1.0 m across inside and 1.2 m deep. About how many litres does it hold? (π = 3.142)
What is the mass of a steel plate 1.0 m × 0.5 m × 6 mm thick? (Steel is 7850 kg/m³.)
A section table gives 50 × 50 × 6 mm angle as 4.47 kg per metre. What is the mass of 14 m of it?
A welding arc runs at 24 V and 150 A. Using power = volts × amps, what is the arc power?
A machine uses 5 kW for 6 hours. Electricity costs J$60 per kWh (a made-up rate for this question). What does the electricity cost?
A job starts at 07:45. It needs 5 hours 50 minutes of work, and there is a 45-minute lunch break. When will it finish?
Each bracket takes 18 minutes to make. How long will 35 brackets take?
Seven cut lengths measure 302, 298, 300, 305, 299, 301 and 300 mm. What is the median length?
Weekly counts of one electrode size in stores were 12, 15, 12, 18, 12 and 15 packets. What is the mode?
A list of gate prices includes one very expensive gate. Which average best shows the usual price?
A calculator gives a cut length of 1247.583 mm. The saw stop can be set to the nearest 0.5 mm. What length is set?
A job works out to need 9.2 sheets of plate. How many sheets should be ordered, and why?
options: 9, because 0.2 of a sheet is too small to count

Drill speed N (rev/min) = (1000 × S) ÷ (π × D), where S is the cutting speed in m/min and D is the drill size in mm. For S = 30 and D = 12, what is N, to the nearest 10 rev/min? (π = 3.142)

How many litres are there in 0.35 m³?

options: The calculator rounded the answer down

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences and show your working. You may use a calculator unless the instructor says otherwise. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: Write 7/16 as a decimal, to four decimal places.
How many millimetres is 2 1/2 inches? (1 inch = 25.4 mm)
What is the name for a comparison of two amounts written like 3 : 4?
A gate costs J$36 000 to make and sells for J$45 000. What is the profit as a percentage of the cost?
Work out 3/4 × 2/3, and give the answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
How many square millimetres are there in 0.5 m²?
A 5 kg box of electrodes costs J$4 750. What is the cost per kilogram, in J$?
What is the mean of 12.4, 12.8, 12.6 and 12.2 mm, in mm?
What is 15% of J$64 000, in J$?
A job starts at 15:40 and takes 2 hours 35 minutes with no break. At what time (24-hour clock) does it finish?
A plate is shaped as a trapezium with parallel sides of 400 mm and 600 mm, 300 mm apart. What is its area in mm²?
A cube-shaped tank measures 1.2 m on each side inside. What is its volume in m³?
A plan says a job needs 4 workers for 9 days. How many worker-days of work is that?

essays.stem: A job needs 4 pieces of 1450 mm and 6 pieces of 850 mm, cut from 6 m bars of the same section. Each saw cut wastes 3 mm. Explain how you would plan the cutting to use as few bars as possible, show your layout, and work out the waste as a percentage of the steel bought.
essays.modelAnswer: First I add up what is needed: 4 × 1450 = 5800 mm and 6 × 850 = 5100 mm, a total of 10 900 mm. With 10 cuts at 3 mm, that is 30 mm more, 10 930 mm, so at least two 6 m bars are needed. I plan the longest pieces first, then fill the gaps with shorter ones. Bar 1: four pieces of 1450 mm use 5800 mm plus 4 cuts × 3 mm = 12 mm, so 5812 mm, leaving an offcut of 188 mm. Bar 2: six pieces of 850 mm use 5100 mm plus 18 mm of cuts, 5118 mm, leaving 882 mm. So two bars, 12 000 mm, are bought. The waste is 12 000 − 10 900 = 1100 mm, including the saw cuts, which is 1100 ÷ 12 000 × 100 = about 9.2%. The 882 mm offcut is long enough to label and keep for another job. I would write this as a cutting plan, one line per bar, so the person cutting can follow it and tick off each piece.
markingPoints: Total length 10 900 mm (10 930 mm with cuts), so at least two bars
Plans the longest pieces first and fills gaps
Correct layout and offcuts: 188 mm and 882 mm
Waste 1100 mm, about 9.2% of the steel bought
Keeps useful offcuts and writes a clear cutting plan

essays.stem: Two welders at J$950 an hour and a helper at J$650 an hour each work 8 hours a day for 3 days on a job. The two welders also work 4 hours of overtime each, paid at time and a half. Work out the total labour cost, showing each step, and explain how you would check it.
essays.modelAnswer: Normal hours for each person are 8 × 3 = 24 hours. Each welder earns 24 × J$950 = J$22 800 at the normal rate, so the two welders together earn J$45 600. The overtime rate is time and a half: J$950 × 1.5 = J$1 425 an hour. Each welder works 4 hours of overtime, so 4 × J$1 425 = J$5 700 each, or J$11 400 for both. The helper earns 24 × J$650 = J$15 600. The total labour cost is J$45 600 + J$11 400 + J$15 600 = J$72 600. To check, I would make a rough estimate: about 80 hours in total at an average of about J$900 is about J$72 000, which is close. I would also add the hours: 24 + 24 + 24 + 4 + 4 = 80 hours, and check that each line on the sheet uses the right rate. Setting the working out as a table, with one line for each person and each type of hours, makes it easy for someone else to check.
markingPoints: Normal hours 24 each; welders J$45 600 at the normal rate
Overtime rate J$1 425 an hour; overtime J$11 400 for both
Helper J$15 600
Total J$72 600
Checks by estimate and by adding hours; sets the working out as a table

essays.stem: Explain the difference between a mark-up and a profit margin. Use a job that costs J$40 000 with a 25% mark-up as your example, and say what price would give a 25% margin instead.
essays.modelAnswer: A mark-up is the profit worked out as a percentage of the cost. A margin is the profit worked out as a percentage of the selling price. They use the same profit, but divide it by a different amount, so the percentages are different. For a job costing J$40 000 with a 25% mark-up, the profit is 25% of J$40 000 = J$10 000, so the selling price is J$50 000. The margin on this job is J$10 000 ÷ J$50 000 × 100 = 20%, not 25%. If the business wants a 25% margin, the cost must be 75% of the selling price. So the price is J$40 000 ÷ 0.75 = J$53 333.33, or about J$53 300. The profit is then J$13 333.33, and 13 333.33 ÷ 53 333.33 is 25%. Mixing the two up can mean pricing too low and losing money. When I price a job I would say clearly which one I am using, and check the answer by working it backwards.
markingPoints: Mark-up is a percentage of cost; margin is a percentage of selling price
25% mark-up: profit J$10 000, price J$50 000
That is a 20% margin
25% margin: price = J$40 000 ÷ 0.75 = about J$53 333
Explains the risk of mixing them up and checks by working backwards

essays.stem: Explain the difference between direct and inverse proportion, with a workshop example of each. Then work out how many workers are needed to finish a 12-day job for 5 workers in 8 days, and say what you would check before relying on the answer.
essays.modelAnswer: In direct proportion, when one amount goes up, the other goes up at the same rate. For example, if 4 brackets use 2.6 kg of electrodes, one bracket uses 2.6 ÷ 4 = 0.65 kg, so 30 brackets use 0.65 × 30 = 19.5 kg. In inverse proportion, when one amount goes up, the other goes down. More workers on the same job means fewer days. A job for 5 workers in 12 days is 5 × 12 = 60 worker-days of work. To finish in 8 days, it needs 60 ÷ 8 = 7.5 workers, so 8 workers must be planned, because you cannot have half a person. Before relying on this, I would check that the work can really be shared, that there is enough space, tools, welding sets and materials for 8 people, and that some tasks do not have to be done one after another, such as waiting for paint to dry. More people may also need more supervision. So the answer is a starting point for the plan, not a promise.
markingPoints: Explains direct proportion with a correct worked example
Explains inverse proportion
60 worker-days; 60 ÷ 8 = 7.5, rounded up to 8 workers
Checks: space, tools and materials for the extra workers
Notes tasks that must be done in order, or supervision, limit the answer

essays.stem: A base plate is 500 mm × 400 mm × 12 mm thick, with four holes 22 mm in diameter. Work out its mass, allowing for the holes, and explain each step. (π = 3.142, steel 7850 kg/m³)
essays.modelAnswer: First I find the area of the plate without holes: 500 × 400 = 200 000 mm². Each hole has a radius of 11 mm, so its area is π × 11 × 11 = 3.142 × 121 = about 380.2 mm². Four holes are 4 × 380.2 = about 1520.7 mm². The area left is 200 000 − 1520.7 = 198 479.3 mm². The volume is this area times the thickness: 198 479.3 × 12 = about 2 381 752 mm³. To change mm³ into m³, I divide by 1 000 000 000, which gives 0.002 382 m³. The mass is volume × density: 0.002 382 × 7850 = about 18.7 kg. To check, the plate without holes would be 0.5 × 0.4 × 0.012 × 7850 = 18.84 kg, and the holes take away only a little, so 18.7 kg makes sense. For lifting and for ordering, I would round this to about 19 kg. Keeping every size in millimetres until the last step, then changing units once, avoids most mistakes.
markingPoints: Plate area 200 000 mm²
Hole area uses the radius: about 380 mm² each, 1521 mm² for four
Volume about 2 381 752 mm³ = 0.002 382 m³, with the unit change shown
Mass about 18.7 kg
Checks against the plate without holes and rounds sensibly

essays.stem: A job has these tasks: mark out 1.25 h, cut 2.5 h, fit and tack 1.75 h, weld 3.2 h, and clean and paint 1.5 h. The working day is 07:30 to 16:00 with a 30-minute lunch. Work out the total time in hours and minutes and when the job will finish if it starts at 07:30 on Monday. Explain any traps in the working.
essays.modelAnswer: First I add the times: 1.25 + 2.5 + 1.75 + 3.2 + 1.5 = 10.2 hours. To change the decimal part into minutes, I multiply by 60: 0.2 × 60 = 12 minutes, so the total is 10 hours 12 minutes. A common trap is to read 3.2 hours as 3 hours 20 minutes; it is really 3 hours 12 minutes. The working day is 07:30 to 16:00, which is 8 hours 30 minutes, less the 30-minute lunch, so there are 8 hours of work each day. On Monday the team works 8 hours, leaving 10 h 12 min − 8 h = 2 hours 12 minutes. On Tuesday they start at 07:30 and finish at 07:30 + 2 h 12 min = 09:42. Another trap is forgetting the lunch break, which would give the wrong finish time. I would also allow for real delays, such as paint drying time or waiting for materials, and tell the customer a finish time with some time to spare.
markingPoints: Total 10.2 hours = 10 hours 12 minutes
Explains converting decimal hours to minutes (3.2 h is 3 h 12 min)
8 working hours a day after lunch is taken off
Finish at 09:42 on Tuesday
Mentions allowing for delays such as drying time

essays.stem: Explain when a figure should be rounded to the nearest value, rounded up, or rounded down. Give a workshop example of each, and explain why rounding too early can cause errors.
essays.modelAnswer: Rounding to the nearest value is used when we need a sensible accuracy, such as a cut length. For example, 1247.58 mm is set as 1247.5 mm if the saw stop reads to 0.5 mm, or 1248 mm on a tape that reads to 1 mm. Rounding up is used when we must have enough of something. If a job needs 4.2 bars or 9.2 sheets, we must order 5 bars or 10 sheets, because a part bar or part sheet cannot be bought. The same applies to the number of workers or packets of electrodes. Rounding down is used when only complete items count. If a bar gives 12.8 pieces, only 12 complete pieces can be cut, and if a budget allows 7.6 hours, only 7 full jobs of 1 hour can be done. Rounding too early, in the middle of a calculation, lets small errors build up. For example, rounding π to 3 instead of 3.142 makes the rim of a ring 1 m across about 142 mm short. So I keep the full figures in the calculator and round only the final answer.
markingPoints: Nearest: for sizes such as cut lengths, with an example
Up: when enough is needed, such as bars, sheets or workers
Down: when only complete items count, such as pieces from a bar
Explains that rounding too early lets errors build up, with an example
Keeps full figures until the final answer

essays.stem: A customer's old drawing shows a stack of three plates, 3/8 inch, 1/4 inch and 5/16 inch thick. Explain how to add these fractions, give the total thickness in inches and in millimetres, and say what you would do about ordering metric plate.
essays.modelAnswer: To add fractions they must have the same bottom number (denominator). The smallest one that 8, 4 and 16 all go into is 16. So 3/8 = 6/16, 1/4 = 4/16, and 5/16 stays as it is. Adding the tops gives 6 + 4 + 5 = 15, so the total is 15/16 inch. To check, I can change each to a decimal: 0.375 + 0.25 + 0.3125 = 0.9375 inch, and 15 ÷ 16 is also 0.9375. To change to millimetres, I multiply by 25.4: 0.9375 × 25.4 = 23.8125 mm, about 23.8 mm. Each plate in millimetres is 9.525 mm, 6.35 mm and 7.9375 mm. Metric plate comes in sizes such as 6, 8, 10 and 12 mm, so the nearest sizes do not match exactly. I would tell the supervisor and the customer, suggest metric sizes such as 10, 6 and 8 mm (24 mm total), and get their approval before ordering, because a change in thickness can affect the fit and the strength.
markingPoints: Uses a common denominator of 16 correctly
Total 15/16 inch, checked with decimals (0.9375 inch)
Converts to about 23.8 mm
Notes metric plate sizes differ and suggests sensible sizes
Gets approval before ordering, with a reason

essays.stem: A welding arc runs at 26 V and 180 A for a total of 3 hours of arc time. The machine is about 80% efficient, and electricity costs J$55 per kWh (a made-up rate for this question). Work out the arc power, the power drawn from the supply, the energy used and its cost, explaining each step.
essays.modelAnswer: The arc power is volts × amps: 26 × 180 = 4680 W, which is 4.68 kW. The machine is about 80% efficient, so only 80% of the power it takes from the supply reaches the arc; the rest is lost as heat in the machine. The power drawn is therefore 4.68 ÷ 0.8 = 5.85 kW. A common mistake is to multiply by 0.8 instead, which would give less power than the arc uses, and that cannot be right. Energy is power × time, so 5.85 kW × 3 hours = 17.55 kWh. The cost is 17.55 × J$55 = J$965.25, about J$965. To check, I can estimate: about 6 kW for 3 hours is about 18 kWh, and 18 × J$55 is about J$990, which is close. This only counts the arc time; the machine also uses some power while it is switched on and idle, so the real cost will be a little higher, and I would use the meter or the maker's figures for a better answer.
markingPoints: Arc power 4.68 kW
Supply power 4.68 ÷ 0.8 = 5.85 kW, with the reason for dividing
Energy 17.55 kWh
Cost about J$965
Checks by estimate and notes idle power makes the real cost higher

essays.stem: A team member hands you this working for a plate 1.2 m × 0.6 m × 8 mm with one 100 mm diameter hole: "Volume = 1.2 × 0.6 × 8 = 5.76 m³. Mass = 5.76 × 7850 = 45 216 kg. Hole area = 3.142 × 100 × 100 = 31 420 mm²." Find the mistakes, give the correct mass allowing for the hole, and explain how you would help the team member avoid such mistakes.
essays.modelAnswer: The first mistake is the units. The length and width are in metres but the thickness is in millimetres, and they were multiplied together without changing. 8 mm is 0.008 m, so the volume is 1.2 × 0.6 × 0.008 = 0.005 76 m³, and the mass is 0.005 76 × 7850 = about 45.2 kg, not 45 216 kg. A rough check would have shown this: a plate a person can lift with help cannot weigh 45 tonnes. The second mistake is the hole area. The formula is π × radius², and the radius is 50 mm, so the area is 3.142 × 50 × 50 = 7855 mm². The hole removes 7855 × 8 = 62 840 mm³, which is 0.000 062 84 m³, or about 0.49 kg. So the plate weighs about 45.2 − 0.5 = 44.7 kg. To help, I would go through the working with the team member, not just correct it. I would show them how to change all sizes to one unit first, write the formula before the numbers, and make a rough estimate to check every answer.
markingPoints: Finds the unit mistake: 8 mm must be 0.008 m
Correct plate mass about 45.2 kg
Finds the hole mistake: uses the radius (50 mm), area 7855 mm²
Correct final mass about 44.7 kg
Helps the team member: one unit, formula first, rough estimate

practical1.title: Plan an optimised cut list and material order for a batch of window grilles, and prove it by cutting one bar
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the team a drawing of a window grille (for example a 1200 mm × 900 mm frame in 25 × 25 mm square tube, with vertical bars at equal spacing and a flat bar decorative strip) and the number needed (for example 6 grilles). As a team, work out on calculation sheets: the cut length and number of every piece; the equal spacing of the bars; a cutting plan that nests the pieces into 6 m lengths with the saw-cut width the assessor gives; the number of lengths to order, the offcuts and the waste percentage; the mass of steel using the section table; the area to be painted; and the cost of materials with the prices the assessor gives, with GCT at the rate the assessor gives shown on its own line. Each member does at least two of these calculations, and a different member checks each one and initials it. Then, under the assessor's supervision, cut one 6 m length exactly to your cutting plan, measure the pieces and the offcut, and compare them with the plan. Present a summary sheet. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and sheets to the group's practical.
materials: The grille drawing, a section mass table and a price list from the assessor
Calculation sheets, squared paper for the cutting plan, and calculators
One 6 m length of the square tube (or a length the assessor chooses)
Steel tape, steel rule, square and scriber or marker
Cold saw or bandsaw (assessor supervised) and clamps
Gloves, safety glasses, ear protection and safety boots for each member
photos: The cut list with lengths and numbers of each piece
The cutting plan for the 6 m lengths, with offcuts shown
Calculation sheets showing working and the checker's initials
The 6 m length marked out to the plan
The cut pieces and offcut laid out beside a tape, with the measured sizes
The summary sheet: lengths to order, waste %, mass, paint area and cost
checklist: Worked out their calculations correctly, with the working and units shown
Checked another member's calculation and found any errors
Planned the cutting to keep waste low, allowing for the saw cut
Rounded correctly (up for ordering, nearest for cut lengths, down for complete pieces)
Marked and measured accurately when proving the cutting plan
Compared the actual pieces and offcut with the plan and explained any difference
Presented results clearly on the summary sheet
safety: Wear gloves, safety glasses, ear protection and boots when handling and cutting steel
Use the saw only under the assessor's supervision, with the work clamped and guards in place
Support long lengths at both ends; lift the 6 m length as a team
Deburr cut ends and keep offcuts off the floor
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Time a small production batch, then cost it and forecast a larger order
practical2.brief: The assessor gives the team a drawing of a simple part that can be made with hand tools and the Centre's machines (for example a flat bar bracket with two holes and a radiused corner) and the materials for 10 of them. As a team, plan the steps (for example mark out, cut, drill, file and check) and share them out so every member works on the batch. Make the 10 parts. One member at a time acts as timekeeper for each step, so every member also records times. Record on a time sheet the start and finish time of every step for every part. Then, on calculation sheets, work out: the total and mean time for each step and for one part, in hours and minutes; the labour cost per part at the hourly rate the assessor gives; the material used per part and the scrap as a percentage; and the total cost per part. Measure each finished part against the drawing and work out the percentage that are within tolerance. Finally, forecast the time, the number of workers and the cost to make 100 parts by a set date the assessor gives, stating your assumptions. Each member presents one part of the results. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and sheets to the group's practical.
materials: The part drawing, the hourly rate and the material prices from the assessor
Flat bar for 10 parts, with marking out tools, hacksaws or the cold saw, pillar drill and files
A stopwatch or phone timer, a time sheet and calculation sheets
Vernier caliper, steel rule and radius gauge for checking
Calculators and a flip chart for the presentation
photos: The plan, showing the steps and who does each one
Members working on different steps, with the timekeeper recording
The completed time sheet for the batch
The 10 finished parts laid out and numbered, with the check results
The calculation sheets for time, cost and scrap
The forecast for 100 parts, presented on the flip chart
checklist: Took part in making the parts safely and to the drawing
Worked out times correctly, including changing decimal hours to hours and minutes
Worked out costs and percentages correctly, with the working shown
Made a sensible forecast for 100 parts and stated the assumptions
Checked results with a rough estimate
Presented their part of the results clearly
safety: Wear safety glasses, boots and the right PPE for each machine; no gloves at the pillar drill
Clamp work for drilling and cutting; use machines only as the Centre's rules allow
Do not rush to beat the clock: safe working comes before speed
Deburr parts and keep the area clear of offcuts and swarf
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
